extracted.intended_audience: general U.S. newspaper readers interested in national politics, labor and post-war policy
extracted.subtask_description: A newspaper news report covering U.S. post‑World War II domestic policy proposals and current labor disputes, including housing surplus use, fact‑finding in strikes, and administrative decisions on military and industry matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surplus housing turnover terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlines terms contemplated for turning over surplus housing to the states: (1) The states to maintain the property. (2) Houses to be rented first to veterans and after that to the general public. (3) Demountable (knocked down) houses in storage areas of various disposal agencies to be erected by the states on favorable federal sites. (4) Leases to be for a maximum of five years with permission to terminate on six months' notice at the end of the housing emergency. (5) Rents in excess of maintenance costs to revert to the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order would authorize the Army and Navy and other owning and disposal agencies to make surplus housing available to the states; the order would include barracks, cantonments, demountable houses and the like. The official said such an authorization could be expected and to be effective at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panelizing temporary war housing (Mead proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to provide $195,000,000 for 'panelizing' war housing — cutting temporary dwellings into panels for transportation and erection in localities needing them. Estimated to provide about 100,000 temporary dwelling units for veterans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government housing experts believe the proposal would help but oppose widespread new building of temporary living quarters because it would simply postpone the need for permanent housing. The proposal was presented as a way to make surplus temporary dwellings usable quickly in localities which need them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taft‑Wagner‑Ellender housing bill features
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending bill would consolidate all Federal housing activities into one agency and establish, as national policy, Government aid to private enterprise and aid in slum clearance; it is described as the 'cornerstone to our nation's post-war reconstruction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labor (William Green) urged provisions enabling private enterprise to bring home ownership within the financial reach of families of moderate income, clear endorsement and rapid enactment of sections to permit resumption of the low‑rent public housing program locally administered. The bill is presented as a 'bold and comprehensive solution.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact‑finding boards for labor disputes (Truman proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: President Truman asked Congress to authorize fact‑finding procedures for important labor disputes, with strikes or lockouts barred for 30 days while the boards operate. He said neither party would be bound by the findings but that making the facts public would usually lead to acceptance of recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Truman proposed appointment of fact‑finding boards (he planned to appoint boards for the GM and steel situations without waiting for Congress). The intent: to avoid work stoppages, make findings public, and in most cases induce acceptance as had occurred in many railway labor disputes. The proposal prompted opposition from some union leaders who saw it as restrictive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible congressional amendments: penalties and arbitration
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee consideration to augment the President's proposal by providing stiff penalties on unions or industries that refused to abide by recommendations and by providing for arbitration machinery; and to repeal major provisions of the Smith‑Connally War Labor Disputes Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: House members indicated willingness to add such measures to bills under consideration so that the President's recommendations could be carried into effect. Action was urged to be swift, ideally before the Christmas recess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Navy reserve release eligibility rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The Navy announced it will release all reserve enlisted men and women 38 years of age or older who had one or more dependents prior to Aug. 15 (with exceptions for regular Navy, those undergoing medical treatment, or under disciplinary action). The wife of an enlisted man is counted as a dependent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimated about 35,000 enlisted personnel in this classification. Many already eligible under the point system; releases do not apply to regular Navy personnel or those ineligible for other stated reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judiciary selection and training proposal (La Guardia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal for a new system of selecting members of the judiciary: provide law candidates a full course, give a test of fundamentals, then two years of postgraduate work; distribute them through departments of State and local government for varied experience; require five to ten years on the lower courts before promotion to courts of unlimited jurisdiction; after 25–30 years assign to the highest courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: La Guardia argued the law profession had shown 'little indication to handle change' and proposed this long-term training/rotation to produce judges with wide experience and a more effective judicial system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for closing alcohol‑based synthetic rubber plants
rubrics_metrics.description: Government decision to close wartime plants producing synthetic rubber from grain alcohol because petroleum‑derived butadiene is far cheaper (about 8–10 cents a pound from petroleum versus about 40 cents a pound from alcohol).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plants at Institute, Kobuta and Louisville that made butadiene from alcohol were being closed or put in 'stand‑by' condition; some plants that actually made rubber from butadiene will continue indefinitely. Economic cost‑effectiveness (dollars and cents) was cited as the controlling criterion; plants and converted refiners would be restored to oil refining condition and kept for emergency use.
